McDonough District Hospital recognized by CMS for zero C. difficile infection rate
N. M. Heil
McDonough District Hospital in Macomb, Illinois, was recognized nationally by the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services for achieving a zero Clostridioides difficile infection rate, according to a June 24 announcement.
CMS data shows that 536 hospitals in the United States reported a C. difficile infection rate of zero based on its healthcare-associated infections dataset. McDonough District Hospital is one of only 15 hospitals in Illinois to reach this milestone. A recent article in Becker’s Hospital Review listed McDonough District Hospital among these facilities.
“A zero C. Diff infection rate is a significant achievement and a testament to the high-quality care that exists at MDH. Preventing healthcare-associated infections requires coordination and commitment across the entire organization. This recognition reinforces our mission to provide exceptional care to our patients. We are very proud of our team,” said MDH Interim Chief Nursing Officer Melissa Onion, RN, BSN, CLC.
Clostridioides difficile, also known as Clostridium difficile or C. diff, is a bacterium that causes diarrhea and inflammation of the colon and is more common among patients in healthcare settings such as hospitals and nursing homes.
Measures used for this recognition were developed by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and collected through the National Healthcare Safety Network from September 2024 to June 2025, with data last updated May 13, 2026. The CDC calculates a standardized infection ratio considering factors such as care location, existing infections among patients, lab methods used, hospital affiliation with medical schools, bed size, patient age and health status.
The Healthcare-Associated Infection measures apply to all acute care hospital patients—including adult, pediatric, neonatal, Medicare and non-Medicare populations—and provide information on infections acquired during hospitalization.
